stories.title: Kidder Mathews Entering Dallas Market
stories.excerpt: Kidder Mathews is expanding into Dallas, Texas, with the addition of six brokers. Mart Martindale, Brandon Beeson, Wilson Stafford, John David Cobb, and Claire Schmeltekopf form an investment sales team, while Barrett Jones joins as a healthcare tenant advisory specialist. The move marks the firm’s first entry into Texas and expands its footprint to 20 offices across six states. The new office will serve the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex and be led by former Edge Capital Markets co-founders Mart Martindale, Brandon Beeson, and Wilson Stafford. Together with Cobb and Schmeltekopf, they have completed more than $3.5 billion in transactions and have valued more than $20 billion in assets. Their clients include KeyBank, EPR Properties Trust, Trigild, BH Properties, Argentic Investment Management, and CWCapital, to name a few. In addition, Barrett Jones joins Kidder Mathews in Dallas, specializing exclusively in healthcare tenant representation. Mart Martindale joins as Senior Vice President, Managing Director, and Shareholder. The post Kidder Mathews Entering Dallas Market appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Kidder Mathews opens first Texas office in Dallas with 6 brokers, $3.5B transaction track record.
Team includes former Edge Capital Markets co-founders; healthcare tenant advisory specialist added.
Expands firm to 20 offices across six states; positions for DFW multifamily brokerage growth.
stories.summary: Kidder Mathews, a major commercial real estate brokerage, is entering Dallas with a 6-person team led by former Edge Capital Markets co-founders Mart Martindale, Brandon Beeson, and Wilson Stafford. The new office will serve the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex and includes a healthcare tenant advisory specialist. The team has completed over $3.5 billion in transactions and valued more than $20 billion in assets, with major institutional clients including KeyBank and EPR Properties Trust.
stories.impact: Brokerage expansion signals confidence in DFW market depth and transaction volume. Multifamily developers should expect increased competitive brokerage coverage, tighter bid-ask spreads on acquisitions, and more sophisticated capital sources entering the market—accelerating both deal velocity and pricing discipline in Dallas-Fort Worth submarkets.

stories.title: Knightvest Capital Acquires 1,027-Unit Round Rock Apartment Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Knightvest Capital acquired the Silicon Hills portfolio, three communities totaling 1,027 units in Round Rock, Texas. Lynd Living was the seller of the three properties. The acquired portfolio includes Enclave at La Frontera, a 411-unit community built in 2004; Lakeside at La Frontera, a 366-unit community built in 2001; and Legends Lake Creek, a 250-unit community built in 2001. Enclave and Lakeside sit adjacent to one another within the La Frontera master-planned mixed-use development in Round Rock, with Legends Lake Creek approximately six miles west in the Lakeline/Lake Creek submarket. Knightvest will implement a comprehensive renovation program, including planned improvements to the exterior, common-area amenities, and a subset of unit interiors. As part of the renovation efforts, Knightvest will rename Enclave at La Frontera to Brixton, Lakeside at La Frontera to Calder, and Legends Lake Creek to Sutton. The post Knightvest Capital Acquires 1,027-Unit Round Rock Apartment Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Knightvest acquires Silicon Hills portfolio: 1,027 units across three Round Rock communities.
Three stabilized assets (built 2001–2004) in La Frontera master-plan and Lakeline submarket.
Comprehensive renovation program planned; portfolio renamed to rebrand aging assets.
stories.summary: Knightvest Capital acquired the Silicon Hills portfolio—three stabilized apartment communities totaling 1,027 units in Round Rock, Texas from Lynd Living. The portfolio includes Enclave at La Frontera (411 units, 2004), Lakeside at La Frontera (366 units, 2001), and Legends Lake Creek (250 units, 2001). Knightvest plans exterior, amenity, and unit-level renovations, along with rebranding the properties as Brixton, Calder, and Sutton.
stories.impact: Value-add acquisition in Round Rock signals sustained demand for Class B/C asset renovation in the Austin metro periphery. Knightvest's rebranding and capex reinvestment suggests confidence in rent growth and NOI expansion; developers should monitor La Frontera master-plan and Lakeline submarkets for infill and ground-up opportunities, as stabilization-stage activity often precedes new supply.

stories.title: Oxford Properties Pays $435M for Fan Pier Office Tower
stories.excerpt: Toronto-based Oxford Properties Group said Wednesday it had acquired One Marina Park Drive, an 18-story Class A office tower located on Fan Pier in Boston’s Seaport District, from Clarion Partners for US$435 million. The deal represents Oxford’s first acquisition of a core office asset in the U.S. in nearly a decade Oxford has spent the past decade diversifying its holdings across major asset classes and recycled approximately US$14 billion out of the office sector globally during the low-rate environment from 2018 to 2022, although it has continued to own high-profile properties in Boston. More recently, it has ramped up office investment, deploying approximately US$2 billion into the sector globally since the start of 2025. “We continue to see compelling opportunities to invest in premier office assets in gateway cities that are well-located, well-amenitized and positioned to benefit from the increasing focus on quality,” said Ankit Bhatt, head of US investments at Oxford Properties. “One Marina Park Drive exemplifies that opportunity. It combines a premier waterfront location, a diverse occupier ecosystem, and exceptional connectivity within one of Boston’s most desirable office districts.” The transaction is believed to represent the highest price paid for a Boston office property since One Lincoln sold in 2006 for $889 million, according to the Boston Business Journal. As a measure of what were then declining office values in Boston, One Lincoln sold at auction for $400 million in early 2025. The post Oxford Properties Pays $435M for Fan Pier Office Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Oxford Properties acquires One Marina Park Drive (Class A office) in Boston Seaport for $435M.
First U.S. core office acquisition by Oxford in nearly a decade; globally deployed $2B into office since early 2025.
Asset located in premier waterfront district with diverse occupier base and strong connectivity.
stories.summary: Toronto-based Oxford Properties Group acquired One Marina Park Drive, an 18-story Class A office tower in Boston's Seaport District, from Clarion Partners for $435 million. This represents Oxford's first U.S. core office acquisition in nearly a decade and reflects a broader pivot: after recycling $14 billion out of office globally from 2018–2022, Oxford has deployed approximately $2 billion back into the sector globally since early 2025, targeting premier gateway assets.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. Oxford's renewed office appetite signals stabilizing cap rates and institutional confidence in Boston and other gateway markets, which can ease overall financing conditions and improve land acquisition climate. However, office capital returning to Boston does not directly compete with multifamily for land or labor in submarkets where multifamily is the primary development focus.

stories.title: Trammell Crow Building Phase II of 2M-SF Houston Industrial Venture
stories.excerpt: Trammell Crow Company and joint venture partner Daiwa House Texas have broken ground on Phase II of Blue Ridge Commerce Center in Houston, Texas. This latest phase, spanning 40.9 acres, will include three speculative buildings totaling 687,000 square feet, with buildings ranging from 182,000 to 303,000 square feet. Phase II is scheduled for a Spring 2027 delivery.The project is located at the northeast corner of Fort Bend Parkway and McHard Road in Fort Bend County, approximately two miles south of Beltway 8. Phase I was delivered last fall. It includes five buildings totaling 1,350,559 square feet. Since its delivery, three of the buildings have been sold to owner-occupants, while another was fully leased. Building 2, a 157,626 square-foot front-load building, remains available. Seeberger Architecture designed Blue Ridge Commerce Center Phase II. E.E. Reed Construction is the general contractor for all Phase II buildings. Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation provided project financing. Cape Bell and Jason Dillee of CBRE are marketing and leasing both phases of the project. The post Trammell Crow Building Phase II of 2M-SF Houston Industrial Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Trammell Crow and Daiwa House break ground on Phase II, Blue Ridge Commerce Center (Houston).
Phase II: 40.9 acres, three spec buildings, 687K SF; Spring 2027 delivery in Fort Bend County.
Phase I delivered fall 2025 (1.35M SF); total project on track for 2M SF industrial hub.
stories.summary: Trammell Crow Company and Daiwa House Texas broke ground on Phase II of Blue Ridge Commerce Center in Houston's Fort Bend County, near the northeast corner of Fort Bend Parkway and McHard Road. Phase II encompasses 40.9 acres with three speculative buildings totaling 687,000 square feet (ranging 182K–303K SF each), scheduled for Spring 2027 delivery. Phase I delivered in fall 2025 with five buildings totaling 1.35 million square feet.
stories.impact: Not applicable to multifamily. Trammell Crow's aggressive industrial spec pipeline in Fort Bend reflects strong logistics demand in the Houston metro and tight industrial supply. While not a direct multifamily play, large-scale industrial construction activity drives regional labor demand and population inflow—supporting underlying fundamentals for multifamily demand in southwest Houston and Fort Bend County submarkets.

stories.title: New York’s 485-x Is Teaching Developers to Stay Below 100 Apartments at a Time
stories.excerpt: In New York City, 485-x is one of the few tools capable of restarting rental construction at a meaningful scale. It is also widely misunderstood because policymakers and developers experience the same incentive in fundamentally different ways. For policymakers, 485-x is a housing production program. For developers, it is a feasibility framework whose thresholds determine what can actually be financed and delivered. Understanding that divergence helps explain the first wave of filings. An analysis of 312 registrations through April 2026 shows that only three projects, or 0.9 percent, contain 100 apartments or more. The other 99.1 percent remain below 100 units, while the median project contains just 24 apartments. Nearly one-third have no more than 10 units. Lev Kimyagarov. DavidBeyda.COM 212-967-6964 Those figures require an important caveat. The registry identifies prospective applicants, not completed buildings, and filing patterns cannot prove intent in any individual project. Still, when projects repeatedly stop at 99 units across separate addresses, the aggregate signal is too consistent to ignore. From a developer’s perspective, the 100-unit line is not an administrative threshold. It is a cost boundary. Under Option A, the commonly selected 35-year exemption paired with a 20 percent affordability requirement, crossing that line brings additional labor obligations. Industry estimates suggest prevailing-wage requirements can increase hard costs by roughly 18 to 28 percent, depending on building type and labor mix. For a typical mid-rise building, that can mean another $45 to $65 per square foot, or $6 million to $12 million on a 120- to 150-unit project. At current borrowing costs and rent levels, the increase can turn a marginally financeable development into one that cannot secure capital. By contrast, dividing a site into two buildings of 70 to 99 units can preserve the tax benefit while avoiding the wage trigger, producing a stronger and more predictable pr
bullets: NYC's 485-x program: 312 registrations analyzed; only 0.9% (3 projects) exceed 100 units.
99.1% of projects filed are sub-100 units; median project is 24 units; 31% have ≤10 units.
Developer behavior reveals 100-unit threshold acts as financing/feasibility cliff, not just policy threshold.
stories.summary: An analysis of 312 registrations filed under New York City's 485-x tax incentive program through April 2026 reveals that only three projects (0.9%) contain 100 or more apartments. The other 99.1% remain below 100 units, with a median project size of just 24 apartments and nearly one-third containing 10 or fewer units. The consistent clustering below 100 units suggests the threshold functions as a hard feasibility constraint for developers, not merely a policy target.
stories.impact: 485-x is fragmenting NYC's rental pipeline into micro-projects. Developers underwriting multifamily in Manhattan and outer boroughs should expect: (1) higher per-unit soft costs and financing friction on smaller deals; (2) delayed rent-up and slower absorption across dispersed properties; (3) reduced economies of scale and property management efficiency. The supply response will be slower and more diffuse than policymakers intended, prolonging NYC's rental shortage and supporting rent growth in the near to medium term.

The eight-story building will include 92,000 square feet of office space and 22,500 square feet of ground-floor retail, designed by renowned firm Snøhetta and built by Kast Construction.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily. The $125M construction financing for a mixed-use office/retail project signals lender appetite for Miami Design District projects and prime Florida CRE. The success of this development could sustain or accelerate mixed-use and retail capex in Miami, but does not affect multifamily supply, demand, or financing fundamentals in South Florida.

stories.title: Investors Are Gaining More Confidence in Office: Survey
stories.excerpt: Investment appetite for office transactions is showing signs of a revival in 2026. Preference from commercial real estate investors for office transactions reached 11 percent in the second quarter. That compares to just 4 percent in early 2025 who listed the office sector as the one with the most opportunities, according to SitusAMC’s latest ValTrends quarterly research report shared exclusively with Commercial Observer ahead of its scheduled release later this week. While office sentiment in the survey was lower than the 16 percent registered in the first quarter, overall trends within the property sector are on the upswing following years of investor confidence in the asset class hovering in the low single digits, said Peter Muoio, head of SitusAMC Insights. Muoio said more clarity on valuations is driving the renewed interest. Increased pressure on some distressed debt may also be a contributing factor behind the numbers, Muoio added. “We’ve been seeing over the past year or year and a half the office investment conditions are improving,” Muoio said. “There is renewed interest.” Part of the increased bullishness toward office investments, according to Muoio, stems from “growing optimism” with the financial feasibility of executing office conversions. The report showed that office cap rates tightened by 10 basis points (bps) in the second quarter, but remained 80 bps above their long-term average. The increasing enthusiasm for office investments in the ValTrends report is part of a more evenly split preference for property types that has been developing over the past year, according to Muoio. Multifamily remained the top-ranked asset class in the second quarter, but optimism cooled in the survey from 60 percent to 36 percent compared to the previous quarter. Muoio said the drop was likely attributed to oversupply issues, particularly in the Sun Belt, taking longer to resolve than initially anticipated. bullets: SitusAMC ValTrends Q2 2026: Office investor preference reached 11%, up from 4% in early 2025.
Still below Q1 2026 level (16%); increased clarity on valuations and distressed debt pressure cited.

stories.summary: Investment appetite for office assets is reviving in 2026, according to SitusAMC's latest ValTrends quarterly research. Investor preference for office transactions reached 11 percent in Q2 2026, compared to just 4 percent in early 2025. While this trails the 16 percent recorded in Q1 2026, it marks a significant upswing from the low single-digit sentiment that prevailed for years. Increased clarity on office valuations and pressure on some distressed debt are driving renewed interest.
stories.impact: Office capital recovery has no direct impact on multifamily underwriting, but signals broader market stabilization and capital availability. Renewed office investor appetite may ease competition for development financing (capital flowing back to office pulls pressure off multifamily markets) and stabilize commercial real estate pricing. Multifamily developers should benefit from moderating cap rate compression and improved leverage terms as overall CRE sentiment strengthens across asset classes.

stories.title: Mexican Restaurant Santo Taco Subleases Former West Village Dig Inn Space
stories.excerpt: Santo Taco is subleasing space formerly occupied by Dig Inn in Manhattan’s West Village, Commercial Observer has learned. The Mexican food concept launched by Santiago Perez in 2025 will take over the 2,800-square-foot, street-level and below-grade space at the Steven Fuchs-owned 232 Bleecker Street at the corner of Bleecker and Carmine streets, according to ManagRE. The sublease runs until 2041. ManagRE did not disclose the asking rent in the off-market deal, but the average asking rent in nearby retail corridors in the Meatpacking District was $252 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE. Navin Bhutani of ManagRE was the sole broker in the deal, and Meerkat Development is managing the buildout of the space. Dig Inn did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Fuchs, who owns a number of properties in the West Village, could not be reached for comment. Santo Taco already has two locations at 114 Kenmare Street and 94 University Place with the new location opening next month. Perez was the CEO of Mexico City-based firm Casamata Hospitality for 10 years, managing concepts like Enrique Olvera’s Pujol as well as Cosme in the Flatiron District and Damian in Los Angeles. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Santo Taco subleases 2.8K SF at 232 Bleecker Street (West Village) from former Dig Inn space.
Sublease runs through 2041; nearby Meatpacking District retail asking at $252/SF in Q2 2026.
Represents third Santo Taco location; off-market deal, rent undisclosed.
stories.summary: Mexican restaurant Santo Taco is subleasing a 2,800-square-foot street-level and below-grade space at 232 Bleecker Street in Manhattan's West Village, taking over the former Dig Inn location. The sublease runs until 2041. The deal was brokered off-market by ManagRE's Navin Bhutani, and nearby Meatpacking District retail was asking $252 per square foot in Q2 2026. This is Santo Taco's third location in New York City.
stories.impact: Not relevant to multifamily development. Retail tenant activity in West Village signals ongoing demand for street-level food and beverage space but does not affect apartment supply, demand, or development feasibility in Manhattan or NYC.

stories.title: Goodland Pickleball Takes 30K SF for New Indoor Clubs in Brooklyn, Queens
stories.excerpt: Indoor pickleball club operator Goodland Pickleball has secured two new club locations in New York City, Commercial Observer has learned. The long-term leases span a total of 30,100 square feet within Class A buildings in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, and Rego Park, Queens. Goodland, which secured its first indoor New York City club in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood in 2024, reports more than 11,000 members across the city. Goodland’s Williamsburg lease, located at Rabsky Group’s 105 North 13th Street, is slated to become its new flagship location. Spanning 14,600 square feet, the club will feature four courts across two floors with 20-foot ceilings, as well as a private fifth-floor court, an outdoor terrace and a sushi bar. The Williamsburg site attracted competition from multiple pickleball operators, Hemant Chavan, founder and CEO of Goodland Pickleball, told CO. Chavan called the site “a needle in a haystack,” estimating that fewer than two dozen indoor spaces suited to pickleball’s lofty space needs exist in the city. Goodland declined to provide the asking rent, but asking retail rents along Bedford Avenue’s nearby North Eighth and North 12th streets corridor averaged $245 per square foot in the latter half of 2025, according to the Real Estate Board of New York (the most recent data available). A rendering of Goodland Pickleball’s planned facility in Rego Park, Queens. RENDERING: Courtesy Goodland Pickleball Goodland represented itself in both lease deals, the second of which landed Goodland 15,500 square feet at RB Realty Capital’s 98-22 Queens Boulevard in Rego Park. The location will accommodate six courts, including a badminton court. Recent asking rents for Queens retail spaces averaged $42.47 per square foot, according to data from CommercialCafe. Both of Goodland’s new sites belong to Class A buildings. bullets: Goodland Pickleball secures 30.1K SF across two NYC club locations: Williamsburg and Rego Park.
Williamsburg flagship (14.6K SF) at 105 North 13th Street; Rego Park location undisclosed size.
Goodland reports 11K+ members across NYC; fewer than 24 Class A sites citywide suit pickleball specs.
stories.summary: Goodland Pickleball, an indoor pickleball operator, has secured two new club locations totaling 30,100 square feet in New York City—one in Williamsburg, Brooklyn (14,600 SF at 105 North 13th Street, a flagship location) and one in Rego Park, Queens. Goodland now operates multiple NYC clubs with over 11,000 members. Founder Hemant Chavan estimates fewer than two dozen Class A spaces in the city are suitable for pickleball's spatial requirements.
stories.impact: Not relevant to multifamily development. Goodland's expansion represents recreational amenity and entertainment demand in outer-borough neighborhoods, but does not affect apartment supply, construction costs, financing, or rental demand. The scarcity of suitable indoor venues may signal underutilized Class A real estate or non-traditional tenant absorption in Brooklyn and Queens, but neither supports nor constrains multifamily development.

stories.title: National Resources Sells New York-Area Mixed-Asset Portfolio for $450M
stories.excerpt: The wait was well worth it. A more than year-long process that began last summer when National Resources CEO Lynne Ward contacted Marty Berger, co-founder of Saber-Hightower, about selling a mixture of commercial real estate assets across the New York City region as part of an estate sale produced a winning result. A joint venture between Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower and Waterfall Asset Management acquired four National Resources properties encompassing more than 4million square feet in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, for $450 million, Commercial Observer has learned. The acquisition, which is anchored by iPark 84, a 270-acre business park in East Fishkill, N.Y., took longer than usual to close given the amount of acreage involving three states, according to Jared Toothman, executive vice president and New York City metro market leader at Lincoln. Toothman said Berger invited him to his golf club to discuss the deal and later added Waterfall to the partnership after pitching the opportunity to investors. “We shook hands on it over a card table at a golf club and then we were off to the races,” Berger told CO. “We took a very long time to really get our hands around a portfolio to be able to extract all the pieces.” The iPark 84 property 50 miles north of Manhattan consists of a 1.8 million-square-foot campus originally developed for IBM’s flagship semiconductor manufacturing plant. It has a diverse tenant mix that includes IBM, Samsung subsidiary eMagin and agricultural company Cal-Maine, and can accommodate 1.5 million square feet of additional development The sale also features a 29-acre, mixed-use center at 761 Main Street in Norwalk, Conn., anchored by a Northwell Health medical outpatient complex, The roughly 400,000 square-foot property includes the corporate headquarters of bicycle company Cannondale, a 70,000-square-foot gym and space for approved multifamily development. The transaction also consists of Edgewater Harbor, in Edgewater, N.J
bullets: National Resources sells NY-area mixed-asset portfolio for $450M to JV: Lincoln Property, Saber-Hightower, Waterfall.
Portfolio: 4M+ SF across NY, NJ, CT; anchored by iPark 84 (270-acre business park in East Fishkill).
Estate sale closed after 1+ year; multi-state complexity extended timeline.
stories.summary: A joint venture between Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower, and Waterfall Asset Management acquired National Resources' mixed-asset portfolio for $450 million. The transaction encompasses four properties totaling over 4 million square feet across New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut, anchored by iPark 84, a 270-acre business park in East Fishkill, New York. The estate sale took over a year to close due to the complexity of coordinating assets across three states.
stories.impact: Not relevant to multifamily development. The iPark 84 business park acquisition signals institutional appetite for industrial and flex real estate in the Hudson Valley and tri-state region, but does not affect multifamily fundamentals. However, large industrial park activity in East Fishkill may support population and wage growth that eventually benefits downstream multifamily demand in regional submarkets.
